%% ------------------------------------------------------------------
%% HESS SHORT SUMMARY (entered in the online submission form; <= 500 characters)
%% ------------------------------------------------------------------
%% GRACE satellites measure changes in water stored on land. We evaluate
%% a simple forecast that filters each basin's storage record before
%% projecting it forward. It improves on damped persistence at most tested
%% lead times in two mascon products. Adding weather history improves
%% forecasts in standardized units, but changes the model ranking when
%% errors are measured in centimeters. These results show why storage
%% forecasts need explicit benchmarks and clearly stated error metrics.
%% ------------------------------------------------------------------

\begin{abstract}
Data-driven forecasts of terrestrial water storage are usually scored by
their agreement with the observations, or against competing models,
rarely against the storage record they start from. How much skill that
record alone supplies is unclear. Persistence, the simplest
such reference, carries forward the latest observed anomaly and its
measurement error. We test whether filtering the GRACE and GRACE-FO record
before extrapolation gives a stronger reference. For each basin we fit a
Kalman filter with a first-order autoregressive state and additive
observation noise, and forecast from the filtered state. Forecasts are
evaluated on deseasonalized anomalies over
% source: Sect. 2.2 basin selection (284 mask basins - 46 ice-sheet - 4 water-body = 234, CSR); Sect. 3.2
% folds (issue starts 2019-06, 2020-11, 2022-04, 2023-09, 2025-02; CSR targets to 2026-05)
234 basins and five expanding-window test periods in 2019--2026. On
the CSR mascon product the filter reduces mean squared error by
% source: results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv, kalman_ar1 rows, skill_vs_damped (0.0498, 0.0879); the
% reference is the stronger of the two damped variants at each lead (scripts/build_paper_ladder.py)
5.0\,\% at a 1-month lead and 8.8\,\% at 2 months, against the stronger
of two damped-persistence references.
% source: results/r0_ablation_summary.csv, rho_estimation_term h1 rmse_a 1.078260 (kalman_r0) against
% results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv damped_persistence_rho h1 rmse_std 1.076129: 1 - (1.078260/1.076129)^2 = -0.0040
Refitting with zero observation-noise variance removes that 1-month gain.
% source: results/jpl/paper_baseline_ladder.csv, kalman_ar1 rows, skill_vs_damped h2..h6 (0.0635, 0.0464,
% 0.0155, 0.0236, 0.0474), all dm_p < 0.02; h1 skill 0.0056, dm_p 0.60
On the JPL product the filter improves on damped persistence at 2--6
months; the 1-month difference is not significant. On CSR, a ridge
regression on 12 months of filtered storage and ERA5-Land variables lowers
standardized error by a further
% source: results/paper_baseline_contrasts.csv, ridge_own_era5_flat12 vs kalman_ar1 h1 (0.0765);
% pooled h1 RMSE in cm (Table C1): KF 5.128, KF-R12E 5.231
7.6\,\% at 1 month, although its pooled error in centimeters is higher
than the filter's. No nonlinear model tested has lower error than this
ridge at 1--3 months. Both the filter and damped persistence have lower
% source: results/phase6_li_comparison_headline.csv and results/jpl/phase6_li_comparison_headline.csv,
% joint_full_cells: at h1 KF vs li_lstm_full +16.4 (CSR, p 2.2e-3) and +43.7 (JPL, p < 1e-3), damped vs
% li_lstm_full +11.9 (CSR, p 0.029) and +43.2 (JPL); GRACE-FCast has significantly lower error than KF
% from h3 (CSR full), h4 (CSR non-seasonal, JPL full) and h5 (JPL non-seasonal)
error than the forcing-driven GRACE-FCast hindcast at 1 month. GRACE-FCast
has significantly lower error than the filter from 3--5 months onward.
Storage forecasts should be scored against a filtered reference and in
physical units.
\end{abstract}

\introduction
\label{sec:intro}

The GRACE and GRACE-FO missions have measured monthly changes in
terrestrial water storage (TWS) since 2002, integrating changes in groundwater,
soil moisture, surface water, snow and ice \citep{tapley2004grace, landerer2020gracefo}.
Anomalies of this quantity (TWSA) have a memory of several months, which
makes them both a forecast target and a source of predictability. TWSA
forecasts support drought early warning and water management
\citep{li2026fldas, arsenault2020nhyfas}, flood-potential assessment
\citep{reager2014flood}, and the bridging of the two- to three-month
latency of GRACE-FO data releases \citep{mo2025nrt}.

A growing number of studies forecast TWSA directly from data. Neural
networks have been trained on GRACE and hydrometeorological series at basin
scale \citep{ahmed2019narx}, at grid scale globally \citep{li2020wrr,
li2024grl, li2026fcast}, for Europe with subsequent assimilation
\citep{li2025wrr}, and for latency filling \citep{mo2025nrt}. Statistical
time-series models have been applied per basin \citep{ahi2021prediction},
benchmark predictability has been quantified at decadal scale
\citep{zhu2019elasticity}, and physically based systems forecast TWS with
seasonal meteorological forcing \citep{li2026fldas, getirana2020groundwater}.
Evaluation differs among these studies. Correlation measures agreement with
observations without specifying a reference forecast, whereas
Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency uses the observed mean as its reference.
\citet{li2024grl} evaluate forecasts against GRACE observations, and
\citet{li2026fcast} compare with SEAS5. Such comparisons do not establish
how much a model improves on the recent storage history. Damped
persistence provides a direct test of that improvement, and of the ten
data-driven TWSA forecasting studies we examined, none reports it.
% source: baseline survey 2026-08-17 (results log entry): li2026fcast full text (SEAS5/GLDAS/WGHM only);
% li2026fldas full text (no reference forecast; lag-autocorrelation diagnostic only); zhu2019 full text
% (elasticity IHC+DCF benchmark); nie2025 full text (AR info excluded by design); steidl2025 (climatology
% + ConvLSTM); li2024grl main text Sect. 4.2 (validation against observations); mo2025nrt, ahmed2019narx (metrics vs observations;
% full texts paywalled); ahi2021 abstract-level.
At sub-seasonal to seasonal leads, the FEWS NET land data
assimilation hindcast of \citet{li2026fldas} concludes that initial
conditions dominate sub-seasonal to seasonal TWS skill, but measures that
dominance with a lag-autocorrelation diagnostic rather than with a
benchmark forecast.

We test whether filtering the storage record gives a stronger benchmark.
Basin-average TWSA is a state variable
observed through a noisy instrument, and the observation errors are large
for small and arid basins \citep{save2016mascons, landerer2020gracefo}. A
persistence forecast starts from the last observed month and propagates
its error, unchanged for raw persistence and attenuated for damped
persistence. The
benchmark we propose is a per-basin Kalman filter \citep{kalman1960} with
a first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) state and additive observation noise.
In this model, noise is any month-to-month variation that the AR(1) state
cannot carry forward: instrument error, but also fast hydrological
variability and errors in the seasonal correction
(Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-kalman}).
The filter separates the persistent signal from this noise before extrapolating, has three parameters
per basin, and needs no data beyond the storage series itself. Because it
propagates its state through months without an observation, it also
remains defined across the eleven-month gap between GRACE and GRACE-FO
without interpolation. Its treatment of missing observations follows from
the state-space model; forecasts issued within that gap are not evaluated here.

The same argument has been made in sea-ice forecasting, where
\citet{niraula2021seaice} showed that damped-persistence references
that ``do not exploit observations optimally'' overstate the skill of
dynamical forecast systems, and built a stronger reference from spatial
damping. Here we follow the same reasoning for satellite-observed TWSA, and strengthen the reference by filtering the storage record. Kalman methods are well established in the GRACE literature, although they have been used for other purposes. For example, ensemble Kalman filters
assimilate TWSA into land-surface models \citep{springer2026review},
forward Kalman filters predict gravity-field coefficients
\citep{kankanige2026persistence}, and integrated postprocessing separates
the non-seasonal signal from noise in the monthly solutions
\citep{zhang2025ipa}. None of these uses a univariate filter on the
finished basin series as a benchmark forecast. A benchmark for TWS prediction has been proposed before by \citet{zhu2019elasticity}, who quantified decadal TWS predictability with an elasticity framework, whereas our benchmark addresses monthly lead times. Most closely related to our work, \citet{nie2025linear} showed on 515 basins that
deep architectures do not beat linear regression for TWS prediction when
autoregressive information is excluded from the feature set by design.
Their design has no lagged storage, so it has neither a persistence nor a
filter benchmark. Our results complement theirs: when lagged storage is included, the
outcome of the model comparison depends more on how the storage record is
filtered than on the choice of architecture.

We compare the filter with persistence and conventional statistical
forecasts, then use ablation experiments to assess the contribution of
its observation-noise term. We also test whether a basin's forcing history
improves the filtered forecast and whether nonlinear models outperform
linear regression on the same inputs. Finally, we compare with the
published GRACE-FCast hindcast \citep{li2026fcast} using two independently
processed mascon products. Section~\ref{sec:data} describes the data,
Sect.~\ref{sec:methods} the forecast target and the models,
Sect.~\ref{sec:results} the results and Sect.~\ref{sec:discussion} their
scope and limits.

\section{Data}
\label{sec:data}

\subsection{GRACE and GRACE-FO mascon solutions}
\label{sec:data-grace}

The primary storage data set is the CSR RL0603M mascon solution
\citep{save2016mascons, save2020rl06} on a $0.25^{\circ}$ grid, April 2002 through May
2026, in centimeters of equivalent water height; the product version is
RL06.2.
% source: raw NetCDF global attrs (title "CSR GRACE and GRACE-FO MASCON RL0603M"; product_version RL06.2), verified 2026-08-13
Each monthly solution is assigned to its official calendar month using the
product's documented list of missing months rather than by the midpoint of
its data span, which would mislabel two solutions.
% source: src/gracefc/basins.py assign_solution_months; results/post_rerun_audit.md sect. 6
The second storage data set is the JPL RL06.3Mv04 mascon solution
\citep{wiese2023jpl} with the
coastline resolution improvement filter applied, sampled at $0.5^{\circ}$,
April 2002 through June 2026, with the product's scale factors applied and
its official missing-month metadata used.
% source: results/jpl/RUN_PROVENANCE.md (product title, version v3.0, DOI 10.5067/TEMSC-3JC634, 0.5-degree sampling, scale_factors_applied=True)
The products have different native estimation geometries. CSR uses
equal-area cells approximately $1^{\circ}$ wide at the equator, whereas
JPL uses approximately $3^{\circ}$ mascons
\citep{csr2026documentation, wiese2023jpl}. These cell sizes and the finer
distribution grids do not represent the effective spatial resolution of
the observations. CSR controls correlated errors through regularized
estimation without additional empirical smoothing or destriping
\citep{csr2026documentation}. We apply no further spatial filter to either
product. The two solutions are independently processed estimates from the
same satellite observations; comparing them tests sensitivity to processing
choices rather than providing independent observational replication.

\subsection{Basins}
\label{sec:data-basins}

Basins follow a HydroSHEDS-based Level-3 basin and mascon partition
\citep{lehner2013hydrosheds}. Each basin series is the cosine-latitude
area-weighted mean of the grid cells in its mask. Of the 284 basins in the
partition we exclude 46 ice-sheet basins in Antarctica and Greenland and
4 water bodies, leaving 234 basins on the CSR product.
% source: docs/STUDY_CONTEXT.md and data/processed/basin_meta.csv (284 mask basins; 46 ice sheets + 4 water bodies excluded; 234 kept)
On the JPL product six small-island masks contain no valid scaled cells,
so 228 basins are kept there.
% source: results/jpl/RUN_PROVENANCE.md (284 mask basins: 228 retained, 46 ice sheets, 4 water bodies, 6 without valid JPL observations)
Figure~\ref{fig:basins} maps the basins and marks the subsets used in the
comparison with GRACE-FCast (Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-li}).

\subsection{ERA5-Land forcing and climate indices}
\label{sec:data-era5}

We use 11 ERA5-Land variables \citep{munozsabater2021era5land} at
$0.5^{\circ}$, regridded server-side from $0.1^{\circ}$, for January 2001
through May 2026: total precipitation, total evaporation, runoff
(total, surface and subsurface), volumetric soil water in four layers, 2-m temperature,
and snow depth water equivalent.
% source: src/gracefc/era5.py variable list; results log era5 ingestion entry (11 variables, unit conversions)
Accumulated fluxes are converted from mean daily rates to calendar-month
totals, the same months to which the storage solutions are assigned
(Sect.~\ref{sec:data-grace}). Evaporation is sign-flipped so that positive
values mean moisture loss, temperature is converted to degrees Celsius, and
snow depth to centimeters of water equivalent. Basin aggregation uses the same cosine-latitude
weighted means as the storage aggregation, mapping each $0.25^{\circ}$
mask cell to its nearest $0.5^{\circ}$ ERA5 cell. Because ERA5-Land is
defined over land only, coastal and island basins aggregate their forcing
from the land fraction of their mask. Of the 234 basins, 79 draw less than
90\,\% of their mask weight from valid ERA5 land cells and 13 less than
50\,\% (minimum 24.5\,\%). No basin is excluded on this ground.
% source: data/processed/era5_basin_coverage.csv over the 234 keep basins (13 < 0.5, 79 < 0.9, min 0.245; verified 2026-08-17)
Twelve monthly climate indices from NOAA PSL enter one benchmark model
only (Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-benchmarks}). Two of them, AMM and PDO, end
before the test window and are dropped from it.
% source: scripts/run_phase2_baselines.py (amm/pdo drop)

\subsection{GRACE-FCast}
\label{sec:data-li}

For the external comparison we use the public GRACE-FCast hindcast of
\citet{li2026fcast}, downloaded from PANGAEA \citep{li2025pangaea}. It is
released as three members built on the JPL, CSR and GSFC mascons. We use
the CSR member against our CSR target and the JPL member against our JPL
target, so that each comparison shares a gravity solution. The CSR member
holds monthly $1^{\circ}$ global forecasts at lead times of 1 to 12 months,
initialized December 2009 through May 2024 (174 initializations), and the JPL member holds 173 initializations through April 2024.
% source: results log, Li ingestion entry (174 init files, 2009-12..2024-05, 1 deg); results/jpl/RUN_PROVENANCE.md (173 files, 2009-12..2024-04)
GRACE-FCast is a long short-term memory network that forecasts the
interannual and sub-seasonal components of TWSA from antecedent
hydrometeorological and oceanographic predictors, with correlation-based
spatial shifting of the predictors. By design it takes no lagged storage
as input, and its seasonal and trend components are extrapolated from the
previous year and added back \citep{li2026fcast}. We evaluate both the
full product and its non-seasonal component (Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-li}).

The skill reported by
\citet{li2026fcast} is for the average of the three members, and their
training-residual diagnostic ranks the CSR member as the least certain of
the three (3.0 against 2.8\,cm), so our results apply to the individual members that we score and not to their three-member average.
% source: docs/reference/li_kusche_2026_core.md sect. 4.1 (JPL 2.8, CSR 3.0, GSFC 2.8 cm)
Their JPL member was trained against JPL RL06.1, whereas our JPL target is
RL06.3Mv04, so the JPL comparison involves two different releases.
% source: results/jpl/RUN_PROVENANCE.md (Li trained on RL06.1_v03; verification target RL06.3Mv04 CRI)
Their training also fills the 2017--2018 mission gap with the
reconstruction of \citet{yin2023gtws}, which is not used by any of our models.

\section{Methods}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{Forecast target}
\label{sec:methods-target}

For each basin and each evaluation fold we fit, on the training window
only, a climatology consisting of a linear trend plus annual and
semiannual harmonics (six coefficients, ordinary least squares). The
frozen coefficients are used to deseasonalize both the training and the
test data, and the residual is divided by its training-window standard
deviation. The forecast target is this deseasonalized, per-basin
standardized residual. It retains interannual and shorter-term anomalies
relevant to drought and flood applications. Standardization expresses each
basin's error relative to its own training variability; it does not impose
equal realized error contributions. Section~\ref{sec:results-weighting} and
Appendix~\ref{app:conventional} report the same forecasts in centimeters,
where basins with larger storage variability contribute more to pooled error.
% source: src/gracefc/evaluate.py deseasonalize_fold (trend + annual + semiannual, train-only fit; train std)

\subsection{Evaluation design}
\label{sec:methods-folds}

We use five expanding-window folds. Their issue windows begin in June
2019, November 2020, April 2022, September 2023 and February 2025, and
together cover June 2019 through April 2026 at a 1-month lead, with
targets reaching May 2026.
% source: src/gracefc/evaluate.py DEFAULT_FOLDS (f1 2019-06..2020-10, f2 2020-11..2022-03, f3 2022-04..2023-08, f4 2023-09..2025-01, f5 2025-02..2026-05)
Fold membership is defined by the forecast issue date. Within each fold,
every climatology, filter parameter, model coefficient and standardization
constant is fit only on observations before the fold's first issue date,
and every test forecast is issued at or after that date. A forecast issued
before the fold start but targeting a month after it belongs to neither
set. Defining membership by target date instead would let a lead-$h$
forecast use transforms fit up to $h-1$ months after its issue date.
Earlier windows are excluded from this common-sample evaluation because
the required lagged predictors are incomplete across the 2017--2018 gap.
Every model is scored on the same rows at
a given lead time, so the sample on the CSR product is
% source: results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv, column n (19422/19188/18954/18720/18486/18252)
$n = 19{,}422$, $19{,}188$, $18{,}954$, $18{,}720$, $18{,}486$ and $18{,}252$
basin-months at lead times of 1 to 6 months. On the JPL product, whose
record runs one month longer, the 228 basins carry 84 issue months at a
1-month lead against 83 on CSR, so
% source: results/jpl/paper_baseline_ladder.csv, column n at horizon 1 (19152 = 228 x 84); results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv n at h1 (19422 = 234 x 83); JPL record to 2026-06 (Sect. 2.1)
$n = 19{,}152$ there. Issue time is defined relative to the last available
observation, so the release latency of GRACE-FO is not modeled and all
results are retrospective potential skill.

\subsection{Benchmark forecasts}
\label{sec:methods-benchmarks}

We evaluate the following benchmark forecasts:
\begin{itemize}
\item climatology, the zero-anomaly forecast;
\item persistence, the last observed anomaly carried forward unchanged;
\item damped persistence in two variants: the $\rho^{h}$ variant
multiplies the last anomaly by a per-basin AR(1) coefficient $\rho$ raised
to the power of the lead time, and the regression variant regresses the
lead-$h$ target directly on the last anomaly;
\item a pooled ridge regression on own-basin lagged anomalies (penalty 1;
lags 0, 1, 2, 5 and 11 months; one model for all basins), and the same
ridge with the lagged climate indices of Sect.~\ref{sec:data-era5} added;
\item a per-basin ridge on the same lags, refit separately for each basin.
\end{itemize}
% source: results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv (model list); src/gracefc/features.py DEFAULT_LAGS = (0,1,2,5,11); src/gracefc/models.py alpha = 1.0
For the comparison reference, we select the damped-persistence variant
with the lower pooled test RMSE at each
lead time: on CSR the $\rho^{h}$ variant at 1 month and the regression
variant at 2 to 6 months, on JPL the $\rho^{h}$ variant at 1 and 2 months
and the regression variant at 3 to 6 months (Appendix~\ref{app:ladder}).
% source: results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv and results/jpl/paper_baseline_ladder.csv, damped_ref column; weaker variant trails by 1.3 % (CSR h1) up to 12.0 % (CSR h5) and 15.0 % (JPL h4)
This retrospective choice provides the more demanding of the two
references; it is not a selection rule available at forecast issue time.
The weaker variant has up to 15\,\% higher mean squared error. Each table
and figure states the reference used.

\subsection{The Kalman filter benchmark}
\label{sec:methods-kalman}

The proposed benchmark models each basin's deseasonalized residual
$y_{t}$ as an AR(1) latent signal $x_{t}$ observed with additive white
noise:
\begin{align}
x_{t} &= \rho\, x_{t-1} + \epsilon_{t}, \qquad \epsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, q),\\
y_{t} &= x_{t} + \eta_{t}, \qquad \eta_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, r).
\end{align}
The three parameters $(\rho, q, r)$ are estimated per basin and fold by
maximum likelihood on training months only, using L-BFGS-B from several
starting points.
% source: src/gracefc/kalman.py fit_kalman_ar1 (MLE, multiple starts, L-BFGS-B)
The filter runs forward through the training and test months and updates
its state estimate $x_{t|t}$ at each observed month with the Kalman gain,
which depends on $\rho$ and on the ratio $q/r$. At a month with no
observation, including the eleven months of the mission gap, the filter
skips the update and propagates its state and state uncertainty forward, so that no interpolation or gap filling is required. The forecast for lead time $h$ issued
at month $t$ is
\begin{equation}
\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \rho^{h}\, x_{t|t},
\end{equation}
which applies damping to the filtered state. We refer to this forecast as
the Kalman filter (KF). The state-space model contains one scalar storage
state per basin and no hydrological model.

We use two variants of the filter to explain its margin over damped persistence. In the \emph{noise-free variant} ($r = 0$) the same model is refit with the same likelihood and with $r$ fixed at zero. This forces
the Kalman gain to one, so the state tracks the raw observation and the
forecast reduces to damped persistence with a maximum-likelihood $\rho$.
The comparison measures the effect of allowing a nonzero observation-noise
variance, including the resulting changes in the fitted state parameters.
% source: src/gracefc/kalman.py fit_kalman_ar1(fixed_r=0.0); scripts/run_r0_ablation.py
In the \emph{two-variance variant} the observation equation has separate
noise variances for months before January 2018 and for GRACE-FO months
from then on, so the parameter vector is $(\rho, q, r_{\mathrm{GRACE}},
r_{\mathrm{FO}})$. We require at least 12 observed GRACE-FO months in the
training window to fit a separate variance; otherwise, the fit uses the
single-variance model.
% source: src/gracefc/kalman_mission.py (MISSION_SPLIT 2018-01-01, MIN_FO_OBS 12); results/kalman_mission_summary.csv diagnostic rows mission_split, min_fo_obs

The split between signal variance $q$ and observation variance $r$ is
set by the likelihood and should not be read as a measurement of
instrument noise. Fast hydrological variability that an
AR(1) state cannot carry forward, and errors in the deseasonalization, are
absorbed into $r$ alongside instrument noise, and in a minority of fits
the likelihood pushes $r$ to its lower bound:
% source: results/kalman_mission_summary.csv, diagnostic rows n_fits 1170 and n_r_one_at_boundary 259
259 of the 1170 basin-fold fits do so. We therefore use ``observation
noise'' in the model's sense, as whatever the filter treats as
unpredictable month-to-month variation, rather than as an estimate of
instrument error.

\subsection{Forecast models built on the filter}
\label{sec:methods-corrections}

We call the following models own-basin models because each uses only
its own basin's storage record and forcing. Every one of them predicts the
error of the Kalman filter forecast, and its own forecast is the filter
forecast plus that predicted error. Table~\ref{tab:names} lists the models and the
abbreviations used for them throughout. In the abbreviations, R denotes a
ridge correction, the number the months of filtered-state history it
uses, and E the ERA5-Land forcing. Four models are linear. KF-R1
regresses the error on the current filtered state alone. KF-R12 regresses
it on the last twelve months of the filtered state. KF-R12E adds the
twelve months of all 11 ERA5-Land anomaly series, giving 12 by 12 features.
KF-R1E instead adds the ERA5-Land anomalies at lags of 0, 1 and 2 months to
the current filtered state. Each ERA5-Land basin series is deseasonalized
with the same train-window trend and harmonic fit as the storage series
(Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-target}), standardized by its training-window
standard deviation and clipped at $\pm 10$ standard deviations before it
enters any model. All four ridges are pooled across basins with penalty 1
on train-standardized features.
% source: src/gracefc/era5.py era5_fold_features (fit_climatology on pre-test months, train std, CLIP_SIGMA)
% source: src/gracefc/experiment_flat12.py (LOOKBACK 12; emit ridge_own_flat12, ridge_own_era5_flat12, kalman_own_ridge); src/gracefc/experiment_nonlinear.py _fit_head (Ridge alpha=1.0); era5_lags (0,1,2)
Three models are nonlinear and use the same information. The LSTM is a
shared-encoder long short-term memory network \citep{hochreiter1997lstm}
over the same twelve-month window of filtered state and the 11 ERA5-Land
channels. It is trained with a time-ordered split that holds out the last
15\,\% of training months for early stopping, and its two seeds are
reported as a seed ensemble. The MLP is a multilayer perceptron (hidden layers of 64 and
32 units, early stopping) on the KF-R12E feature vector, with two seeds.
The residual MLP is a two-stage model, KF-R1E followed by an MLP of the
same size trained on the first stage's training residual, with three
seeds.
% source: src/gracefc/experiment_lstm.py (12-month window, 85/15 split, seeds 0-1); experiment_nonlinear.py mlp head (64,32, early stopping); experiment_resmlp.py (3 seeds)
Finally, two neighbor models, not adopted
(Sect.~\ref{sec:results-dropped}), add to KF-R1 the filtered state of one
other basin propagated to the target month, with that basin chosen by
correlation or by distance.
% source: src/gracefc/graphs.py (correlation- and distance-selected neighbor); results/phase3b_summary.csv (kalman_corr_top1, kalman_geo_top1)
Five of these forecasts are also reported in centimeters
(Sect.~\ref{sec:results-weighting} and Appendix~\ref{app:conventional}):
the stronger damped-persistence variant, KF, KF-R1, KF-R12 and KF-R12E.
% source: scripts/compute_conventional_metrics.py (the five retained systems; DAMPED_BY_H rho at h1, reg at h2-h6)

\subsection{Comparison with GRACE-FCast}
\label{sec:methods-li}

The GRACE-FCast hindcast \citep{li2025pangaea} is aggregated to our basin
geometry with exact $0.25^{\circ}$ to $1^{\circ}$ cell-containment
weights. Its forecasts are moved into each fold's deseasonalized,
standardized space using our train-window climatology plus a per-fold,
per-basin, per-lead mean offset estimated on pre-test data only. The full
product is scored after our climatology is subtracted, so any difference
between their seasonal and trend convention and ours is absorbed there.
The non-seasonal component, which is their interannual plus sub-seasonal
forecast, is scored in the same space, which removes the advantage that
their monthly re-extrapolation of the seasonal cycle and trend would
otherwise carry. Every model is scored on the identical set of basin-months at every lead
time. On CSR it spans 60 test months: folds
1 to 3 in full, 9 of the 17 issue months of fold 4, and none of fold 5,
because GRACE-FCast's final initialization, May 2024, falls inside fold 4.
On JPL, whose final initialization is one month earlier, it spans 59
months.
% source: results/phase6_li_comparison_headline.csv (n_months 60 = 17+17+17+9); results/jpl/phase6_li_comparison_headline.csv (n_months 59 = 17+17+17+8);
% src/gracefc/evaluate.py DEFAULT_FOLDS (fold 4 issue window 2023-09..2025-01); Sect. 2.4 (final initializations 2024-05 CSR, 2024-04 JPL)

We define two basin sets. The matched set keeps every basin with at least
one usable GRACE-FCast cell, which is 227 of the 234 basins on CSR and 227
of 228 on JPL.
% source: results/phase6_li_comparison_summary.csv (all_matched n_basins 227); results/jpl/phase6_li_comparison_summary.csv (all_matched n_basins 227)
The fully covered set applies one rule to both products: a basin enters
only if it fully contains every $0.25^{\circ}$ mask cell of at least one
native mascon of the product being scored, and all sixteen cells of at
least one finite $1^{\circ}$ GRACE-FCast cell. This rule tests cell containment directly and does not rely on an area or coverage threshold. On CSR, 229 basins
contain a full native mascon, 211 contain a full forecast cell, and 209 satisfy both. On JPL, whose native mascons are coarser on the sampled grid,
67 do. The rule screens grid geometry only: a single native mascon is not
an independently resolved gravity signal, because the effective resolution
of the observations is coarser than the mascon and the regularized
estimation couples neighboring mascons (Sect.~\ref{sec:data-grace}).
% source: data/processed/li2026_basin_coverage.csv (n_full_native_mascons >= 1: 229; n_full_li_cells >= 1: 211; both: 209); results/jpl/phase6_li_comparison_summary.csv (joint_full_cells n_basins 67)
We report the fully covered set. On the matched set, the standardized
1-month error of the full product on JPL is
% source: results/jpl/phase6_li_comparison_summary.csv, li_lstm_full rmse_std h1: all_matched 5.471, joint_full_cells 0.926
5.47 against 0.93 on the fully covered set. The gap arises because our
standardization uses the residual standard deviation of our own product,
which is small in basins that the coarser forecast grid only partly
covers. Values on the matched set are therefore dominated by grid mismatch, and we do not interpret them as forecast accuracy.

\subsection{Verification statistics}
\label{sec:methods-stats}

The primary metric is the pooled root-mean-square error (RMSE) in
standardized units. We report it as the mean-squared-error skill score of
a forecast $A$ against a stated benchmark $B$,
\begin{equation}
S_{A|B} = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{MSE}_{A}}{\mathrm{MSE}_{B}},
\end{equation}
in percent, so that a positive value means $A$ has the lower error. The
forecast and reference are stated for each comparison.
Pooled comparisons use the Diebold--Mariano test
\citep{diebold1995comparing} on the monthly cross-basin mean loss
differential, with the small-sample correction of
\citet{harvey1997testing} and a Newey--West variance at maximum lag
$\max(h-1, 1)$ \citep{newey1987hac}. Confidence intervals use a
moving-block bootstrap \citep{kunsch1989blockboot} of the monthly losses
with block length $\max(3, h)$ and 2000 draws, so that the block covers
the lag-$(h-1)$ dependence of overlapping $h$-step forecasts.
% source: src/gracefc/stats.py diebold_mariano (HAC max_lag = max(h-1,1)) and block_bootstrap_skill_ci (block = max(3, horizon), n_boot 2000)
Per-basin significance uses per-basin Diebold--Mariano statistics on the
scored test months with Benjamini--Hochberg false-discovery-rate control at
$q = 0.10$ \citep{benjamini1995fdr}, following the field-significance
reasoning of \citet{wilks2016stippling}. Basins that are helped and basins
that are hurt are always counted separately. In the text we state whether a
difference is significant at $p < 0.05$. Tables report two-sided $p$
values, with values below 0.001 written as $<0.001$. A small $p$ value
indicates a difference in mean loss; the sign of the skill score identifies
which forecast has lower error. Pooled tests are not adjusted across model
and lead-time comparisons; false-discovery-rate correction applies only
to the stated families of per-basin tests.

\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Why the filter improves on damped persistence}
\label{sec:results-mechanism}

We use two ablation experiments to identify the source of the margin (Fig.~\ref{fig:mechanism}). The
noise-free variant, the same model refit with $r = 0$, loses to the full
filter at every lead time, by
% source: results/r0_ablation_summary.csv, noise_filtering_term rows, skill_pct (5.35, 9.63, 11.67, 12.48, 12.65, 12.27) and dm_p (max 7.2e-14 at h1)
$5.35\,\%$ at 1 month, rising to $12.65\,\%$ at 5 months ($p < 0.001$
at every lead time). Scored against the regression variant at every lead
time, the noise-free variant is
% source: results/r0_ablation_summary.csv, rho_estimation_term rows, skill_pct (0.90, -0.93, -6.84, -10.75, -11.57, -9.85) and dm_p (1.6e-5, 0.0022, ...)
$+0.90\,\%$ ahead at 1 month and $0.93$ to $11.57\,\%$ behind at 2 to 6
months; against the $\rho^{h}$ variant, the stronger one at 1 month, it is
% source: results/r0_ablation_summary.csv, rho_estimation_term h1 rmse_a 1.078260 (kalman_r0); results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv, damped_persistence_rho h1 rmse_std 1.076129; 1 - (1.078260/1.076129)^2 = -0.0040
$0.40\,\%$ behind. At a 1-month lead time the AR(1) structure without the
noise term is therefore within 1\,\% of damped persistence in either
direction. The corresponding mean-squared-error ratios multiply:
$0.9465 \times 1.0040 \simeq 0.9502$, recovering the $4.98\,\%$
improvement in Table~\ref{tab:ladder}. Allowing a nonzero observation-noise
variance accounts for the improvement within this model family.
% source: (1 - 0.05354) x (1.078260/1.076129)^2 = 0.94646 x 1.00397 = 0.95021 = 1 - 0.0498; results/r0_ablation_summary.csv and results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv as above
Because $r$ absorbs whatever an AR(1) state cannot carry forward
(Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-kalman}), the ablation attributes the margin to
filtering within the model class rather than to a particular physical
noise source.

The second ablation asks whether the margin depends on treating GRACE and
GRACE-FO as one instrument. The two-variance variant, with a separate
observation variance for GRACE-FO months, is worse than the
single-variance filter at every lead time:
% source: results/kalman_mission_summary.csv, mission_split_term rows, skill_pct (-1.84, -0.80, -0.65, -0.57, -0.53, -0.38) and dm_p (1.7e-7, 1.1e-4, 2.7e-4, 5.3e-4, 0.0020, 0.0060425)
$-1.84\,\%$ at 1 month ($p < 0.001$) and $-0.80$ to $-0.38\,\%$ at 2 to
6 months ($p < 0.01$). Per basin at a 1-month lead time, after
false-discovery-rate control, none of the 234 basins has a significant
improvement or deterioration. The pooled difference is therefore not
accompanied by individually significant basin differences.
% source: results/kalman_mission_summary.csv, diagnostic rows perbasin_h1_helped_bh 0, perbasin_h1_hurt_bh 0, perbasin_h1_n_tested 234
The first fold's training window ends in May 2019 and holds fewer than
12 GRACE-FO months, so all 234 of its basin-fold fits fall back to the
single variance (Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-kalman}).
% source: results/kalman_mission_summary.csv, diagnostic row n_fallback_r_fo 234 (of n_fits 1170)
Every scored month is a GRACE-FO month. The separate GRACE-FO variance is
estimated from fewer than seven years in any fold, which may limit its
precision. The single-variance filter has lower test error and is retained
for the remaining comparisons.

\subsection{Forecast models built on the filter}
\label{sec:results-flat12}

Table~\ref{tab:corrections} scores the own-basin models against the
filter. KF-R1, which adds one regression coefficient on the current
filtered state, is weaker than KF at 1 and 2 months, by
% source: results/flat12_ridge_summary.csv, kalman_own_ridge rows, skill_vs_kalman x100 (h1 -0.17, h2 -1.01) and dm_p_vs_kalman (1.8e-6, 1.9e-11)
$-0.17$ and $-1.01\,\%$, and stronger at 3 to 6 months, by
% source: results/flat12_ridge_summary.csv, kalman_own_ridge rows, skill_vs_kalman x100 (h3 0.44, h4 2.36, h5 2.66, h6 1.59) and dm_p_vs_kalman (1.1e-14, 1.6e-13, 5.9e-14, 2.3e-17)
$+0.44$ to $+2.66\,\%$ ($p < 0.001$). Both use the same current filtered
state and require only the storage record.
KF-R12, which uses twelve months of the filtered state instead
of one, improves on KF at every lead time, by
% source: results/paper_baseline_contrasts.csv, ridge_own_flat12 vs kalman_ar1 (skill x100: 0.81, 1.48, 1.76, 1.81, 1.49, 0.63; dm_p 0.0035, 4.9e-6, 2.9e-10, 7.5e-10, 3.4e-7, 0.015158)
$+0.63$ to $+1.81\,\%$ ($p < 0.02$). KF-R12E adds the twelve-month forcing
window and gains
% source: results/paper_baseline_contrasts.csv, ridge_own_era5_flat12 vs kalman_ar1 (skill x100: 7.65, 5.39, 4.22, 3.19, 2.09, 0.87; ci h1 4.7..10.1; dm_p 1.1e-8, 1.1e-8, 3.0e-8, 5.2e-6, 9.0e-4, 0.12)
$+7.65\,\%$ over KF at 1 month (95\,\% interval $+4.7$ to $+10.1\,\%$),
a gain that falls from $+5.39\,\%$ at 2 months to $+2.09\,\%$ at 5
months ($p < 0.001$), and a
non-significant $+0.87\,\%$ at 6 months ($p = 0.12$). Relative to damped
persistence this is
% source: results/paper_baseline_ladder.csv, ridge_own_era5_flat12 rows, skill_vs_damped x100 (12.24, 13.71, 9.61, 6.16, 4.58, 4.47)
$+12.2\,\%$ at 1 month and $+13.7\,\%$ at 2 months (Table~\ref{tab:ladder}),

(Appendix~\ref{app:ladder}). The forcing window improves on KF-R1 only up

The gain from the forcing window is not uniform across basins.
Figure~\ref{fig:era5where} maps the per-basin 1-month skill of KF-R12E
over KF and plots it against each basin's median training-window storage
standard deviation across folds. The relation is weak across the sample
% source: scripts/make_figures.py fig05_era5_where (Spearman rho -0.1436, p 0.028, n 234; BH q = 0.10: 45 significant, 44 helped, 1 hurt; std range of the significant basins in figures/BUILD_NOTES.md)
(Spearman $\rho = -0.14$). The 45 basins that are significant under
false-discovery-rate control, 44 helped and 1 hurt, all have
training-window standard deviations below 9\,cm, and none of the
highest-variance basins gains significantly. One standardized unit
represents a smaller physical anomaly in a low-variance basin. Improvements
there contribute more to the standardized comparison than to pooled error
in centimeters. This scaling makes the ranking of the
models sensitive to how basins are weighted
(Sect.~\ref{sec:results-weighting}).

None of the nonlinear models improves on KF-R12E given the same twelve
months of history (Table~\ref{tab:sequence} and Fig.~\ref{fig:sequence}).
At 1 to 3 months KF-R12E has the lowest standardized RMSE of every model
and seed. The MLP, which sees the identical feature vector, is
significantly worse in every seed at every lead time
% source: results/phase7_lstm_summary.csv, mlp_own_era5_flat12_s0/s1 rows, dm_vs_ridge_twin (positive = worse than twin) and dm_p (h1 1.9e-10, 1.1e-6; h2 2.3e-6, 4.1e-8; h3 5.5e-7, 8.3e-13); max = 2.3e-6
($p < 0.001$), and the residual MLP and both LSTM seeds fall between
KF-R12E and KF-R1E. Because the LSTM holds out the last 15\,\% of its
training months for early stopping, its comparison with a ridge fit on all
training months is not matched on training data. We therefore refit
KF-R12E on the LSTM's training months. Against the two-seed LSTM ensemble
the refit ridge is ahead by
% source: results/flat12_train85_sensitivity.csv, ridge_own_era5_flat12_train85 vs lstm_own_era5_ens (skill_pct 1.02, 2.76, 2.27; dm_p 0.094, 2.7e-10, 4.3e-9)
$+1.02\,\%$ at 1 month ($p = 0.094$), $+2.76\,\%$ at 2 months and
$+2.27\,\%$ at 3 months (both $p < 0.001$). Its difference
from the ridge fit on all months is not significant
% source: results/flat12_train85_sensitivity.csv, ridge_own_era5_flat12_train85 vs ridge_own_era5_flat12 (skill_pct -0.17, 0.04, 0.19; dm_p 0.50, 0.83, 0.1925)
(differences within $0.2\,\%$, $p \ge 0.19$). Under the architectures and
training budget tested on CSR, the nonlinear models provide no improvement
over this linear representation of the storage and forcing history.

At the level of individual basins, the 1-month result is close to an even split, and the number of basins in which GRACE-FCast is better increases with lead time. On CSR the full product has the lower
error in
% source: results/phase6_li_comparison_perbasin.csv, li_lstm_full vs kalman_ar1, a_better by horizon (98, 137, 149, 153, 156, 157 of 209)
98 of the 209 basins against KF at 1 month and in 157 at 6 months, and in
% source: results/phase6_li_comparison_perbasin.csv, li_lstm_full vs ridge_own_era5_flat12, a_better by horizon (87, 133, 147, 151, 159, 162 of 209)
87 against KF-R12E at 1 month and 162 at 6 months. The pooled 1-month
margin therefore reflects large gains in a subset of basins and not a consistent advantage across basins.

The short-lead comparison is sensitive to the available inputs.
GRACE-FCast takes no lagged storage as input, whereas damped persistence,
KF and its corrections use the recent storage record. Damped persistence
has lower error than the full product at 1 month, by
% source: results/phase6_li_comparison_headline.csv, joint_full_cells, damped_persistence_rho vs li_lstm_full (skill x100: 11.9, -16.9, -30.9, -42.2, -47.9, -54.3; dm_p 0.029, 1.1e-3, ...)
$+11.9\,\%$ on CSR and
% source: results/jpl/phase6_li_comparison_headline.csv, joint_full_cells, li_lstm_full vs damped_persistence_rho, stored s -0.7609 (h1), -0.0424 (h2, dm_p 0.49), +0.1597 (h3, dm_p 0.0047)
$+43.2\,\%$ on JPL, and loses to it from 2 months on CSR and from 3 months
on JPL (Table~\ref{tab:li}). The comparison with damped persistence more
directly assesses the contribution of filtering. On the full benchmark
sample, the 1-month improvement is $+5.0\,\%$ on CSR
(Table~\ref{tab:ladder}), with no significant difference on JPL
% source: results/jpl/paper_baseline_contrasts.csv, kalman_ar1 vs damped_persistence_rho h1 (skill 0.0056, dm_p 0.60)
($+0.6\,\%$, $p = 0.60$; Sect.~\ref{sec:results-ladder}). The 1-month
margin over the product is much larger on JPL than on CSR. The fully
covered JPL set contains 67 basins selected by native-cell containment, and the
JPL member of GRACE-FCast was trained on an earlier release than the one
we score it against (Sect.~\ref{sec:data-li}). We cannot separate these two effects.

\subsection{Sensitivity to basin weighting}
\label{sec:results-weighting}

The comparisons above use basin-standardized errors. In pooled
centimeter errors, high-variance basins contribute more to squared error. The
five forecasts reported in that unit differ by about half a centimeter at
most, and the differences among the filter-based models are untested (Fig.~\ref{fig:ladder}b; Appendix~\ref{app:conventional}).
KF-R12 has the lowest value at 1 to 3 months and KF-R1 at 4 to 6 months,
and KF-R12E, the best model in standardized units, is
% source: results/conventional_metrics_summary.csv, pooled_rmse_cm h1: ridge_own_era5_flat12 5.231, kalman_ar1 5.128, ridge_own_flat12 5.118; kalman_own_ridge lowest at h4-h6 (6.064, 6.288, 6.603)
0.1\,cm behind the filter at 1 month. Damped persistence has the highest
RMSE at every lead time in this weighting as well.
% source: results/conventional_metrics_summary.csv, pooled_rmse_cm: damped_persistence (5.321, 6.156, 6.383, 6.447, 6.689, 6.935)
The filter's margin over persistence therefore does not depend on the
weighting, but the gain from the forcing window does. It is concentrated in the low-variance basins of Fig.~\ref{fig:era5where}, which receive full weight in the standardized metric and little weight in the centimeter metric. Any ranking of models on this target should therefore state the weighting used. In this paper, ``best own-basin model'' means lowest pooled
standardized error.

\subsection{Neighboring-basin predictors}
\label{sec:results-dropped}

Spatial and graph-based TWSA methods assume that one basin's history helps
forecast another's future: \citet{li2026fcast} shift predictors across
space, \citet{arzoumanidis2026stgnn} build a proximity and correlation
basin graph for reconstruction, and \citet{steidl2025hignn} forecast with
a hierarchical basin graph. We tested the simplest version of that
assumption: whether one other basin's filtered state, propagated to the
target month and added as a feature to KF-R1, improves the forecast. On
CSR a correlation-selected neighbor was worth
% source: results/phase3b_summary.csv, kalman_corr_top1 h1, skill_vs_own_ridge 0.0031, placebo_beaten 50 of 50; results/phase4_surrogate_summary.csv h1 beats_n_of 99/99
$+0.31\,\%$ over KF-R1 at 1 month, ahead of all 50 seed-matched random
neighbor graphs and all 99 amplitude-adjusted Fourier-transform surrogates
\citep{schreiber1996surrogate}, and nothing at 2 to 6 months. None of this is reproduced on JPL. There, every neighbor variant is worse than KF-R1 at every lead time. The correlation-selected neighbor beats none of the 50 random
graphs at any lead time, the distance-selected neighbor beats at most 26
of 50, and the real graph beats none of the 99 surrogates.
% source: results/jpl/phase3b_summary.csv, kalman_corr_top1 rows, skill_vs_own_ridge x100 (-0.52 .. -1.28), placebo_beaten 0 of 50 at every lead; kalman_geo_top1 placebo_beaten (0, 0, 0, 8, 26, 9 of 50); results/jpl/phase4_surrogate_summary.csv, beats_n_of 0/99 at every lead
The reversal across processing centers provides no support for adopting
this neighboring-basin correction as a general improvement.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{What the benchmark means for reported skill}
\label{sec:disc-benchmark}

Filtering improves the use of recent storage history as a forecast
benchmark. In this evaluation, a three-parameter filter has lower error
than both persistence variants on CSR and at most tested leads on JPL
(Table~\ref{tab:ladder}; Appendix~\ref{app:ladder}). A model's improvement
over climatology or raw persistence therefore does not establish an
improvement over the information available from the storage record.
The size of this difference depends on the target, product, and lead time.
The percentages reported here cannot be added across reference forecasts
or used to adjust skill reported in other studies without evaluating
their predictions on a common target.

In physical units the margin is modest. At a 1-month lead time the pooled
RMSE falls from
% source: results/conventional_metrics_summary.csv, h1 pooled_rmse_cm damped_persistence 5.321 -> kalman_ar1 5.128; rmse_cm_med 2.74 -> 2.66
5.32 to 5.13\,cm of equivalent water height and the per-basin median from
2.74 to 2.66\,cm (Appendix~\ref{app:conventional}). The gain is largest
where the anomaly is small and the observation noisy
(Fig.~\ref{fig:mechanism}c), which are the arid and small basins in which
GRACE-based drought indicators are least certain \citep{save2016mascons}.
In large humid basins such as the Amazon, the filter and damped persistence
are nearly the same forecast (Fig.~\ref{fig:examples}d). The benchmark
therefore changes the accounting of learned skill more than it changes the
error of the basins that dominate centimeter metrics.

GRACE-FCast has lower error at longer lead times in the external
comparison. On the fully covered CSR sample, KF and KF-R12E have
% source: results/phase6_li_comparison_headline.csv, joint_full_cells, the four pairs of Table 5 at h4-h6, ours first (-10.1 to -35.4)
10 to 35\,\% higher mean squared error than the full or non-seasonal
GRACE-FCast forecast at 4 to 6 months. At 1 month, KF, KF-R12E and damped
persistence have lower error than the full product; at 2 months, KF also
has lower error than its non-seasonal component. These comparisons require
an explicit reference forecast and cannot be inferred from full-signal
correlation alone. \citet{li2026fcast} report a related sensitivity to
the verification target: they find
correlation above 0.8 over about 72\,\% of global land at a 1-month lead
time for the full signal but over only 20\,\% once the seasonal cycle and
trend are removed. They attribute the difference to the extrapolated
components.
% source: docs/reference/li_kusche_2026_core.md sects. 5.1 and 6.1 (CC > 0.8 land fraction 72% full, 20% non-seasonal at lead 1; three-product mean)
Appendix~\ref{app:conventional} likewise shows higher correlations after
the extrapolated seasonal cycle and trend are restored to our forecasts.
Reporting full-signal metrics alongside deseasonalized skill makes clear
whether a model improves the less predictable residual component.

Our result complements that of \citet{nie2025linear}
(Sect.~\ref{sec:intro}), who compare architectures with lagged storage
excluded. Here, a linear correction using filtered storage and forcing
has lower CSR error than the nonlinear models tested on the same inputs
(Sect.~\ref{sec:results-flat12}). The training-matched comparison retains
this advantage over the LSTM at 2 and 3 months, but the 1-month difference
is not significant. This supports retaining linear models as controls in
architecture comparisons. It does not establish their superiority under
other training budgets or on other targets. In particular, simulated,
reconstructed and gap-filled targets, including HydroGlobe
\citep{nie2025linear} and the products of \citet{humphrey2019gracerec},
\citet{yin2023gtws} and \citet{mo2022gap}, have error structures that differ
from direct mascon observations. The benefit of filtering those targets
would need to be evaluated separately.

\subsection{Initial conditions versus forcing}
\label{sec:disc-crossing}

Seasonal hydrological forecasting experiments distinguish predictability
from initial conditions and meteorological forcing. Initial conditions
often contribute most at short leads, with forcing becoming more
important as lead time increases \citep{wood2008esp,
shukla2011seasonal, koster2010glace2, yossef2013skill,
pechlivanidis2020drivers}. Those results were established for streamflow
and soil moisture in ensemble streamflow prediction experiments. The
comparison in Sect.~\ref{sec:results-li} is consistent with this pattern:
KF has lower error at short leads, whereas GRACE-FCast has significantly
lower error from 3 to 5 months onward, depending on the product and
component (Table~\ref{tab:li}). The 1-month advantage also occurs for
damped persistence. The crossover describes these forecast systems; it
does not decompose skill into contributions from storage and forcing.
Architecture, training data, gap treatment, predictor sets and target
decomposition differ together in this comparison.

The own-basin ERA5-Land history improves the CSR linear correction through
4 months relative to KF-R1 (Sect.~\ref{sec:results-flat12}), while the
external product retains its advantage over KF through the longest lead
evaluated. These results motivate combining storage-based and forcing-based
forecasts. A switching lead or blending weight would need to be selected
and evaluated on separate data; the crossings in Fig.~\ref{fig:crossing}
do not by themselves establish such a rule.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:disc-limitations}

None of our models uses forecast forcing; the ERA5-Land window ends at the
issue month. The comparisons therefore concern predictability from
antecedent observations and reanalysis. They do not assess the benefit of
adding meteorological forecasts.

Observation latency changes the operational meaning of these lead times. GRACE-FO
solutions are released two to three months after the observation month
\citep{mo2025nrt}. Predicting next month's storage from an observation
released two to three months late requires an observation-relative lead
of approximately 3 to 4 months. On CSR, those leads are at or beyond the
crossover with GRACE-FCast. The common issue-date convention used here
supports retrospective comparison; it does not reproduce the availability
of all inputs in an operational forecast.

The cross-product evidence reported here concerns the benchmark forecasts
and their comparison with GRACE-FCast. The detailed correction-model
ranking in Sect.~\ref{sec:results-flat12} is for CSR and should not be
generalized to JPL. The fully covered JPL set contains 67 basins selected
by native-cell containment, and the JPL member
of GRACE-FCast was trained on an earlier release than we score it against.
For that reason the size of the 1-month margin there should not be
compared with CSR's.
In addition, the filter's 1-month margin over damped persistence does not
replicate on JPL: no significant difference is detected at 1 month, while
KF improves on damped persistence at 2 to 6 months
(Sect.~\ref{sec:results-ladder}). The smaller JPL persistence error is
consistent with less unpredictable month-to-month variation, but the
contribution of individual processing choices was not isolated.

All results are for basin averages. Most published data-driven TWSA
forecasts are gridded \citep{li2020wrr, li2024grl, li2026fcast}. Spatial
aggregation changes both the signal and its error structure, so the
filter's performance at grid scale remains to be tested, with
$(\rho, q, r)$ estimated for each cell.

The filter's definition across the 2017--2018 gap follows from its
prediction step, which runs whenever an update is skipped. However, no scored forecast is issued across the gap (Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-folds}), so this
property is not tested here. Similarly, the noise term is not identified
as instrument noise: 259 of 1170 basin-fold fits push $r$ to its lower
bound (Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-kalman}), and the AR(1) plus white-noise
decomposition absorbs unmodeled dynamics into $r$. The ablation attributes
the margin to filtering within the model class, and what is filtered out is a
mixture of instrument noise and fast hydrology whose shares we do not
estimate.

The ranking of models above the filter depends on basin weighting. The
forcing window's gain is concentrated in low-variance basins that contribute
less to pooled centimeter error (Sect.~\ref{sec:results-weighting}), while
the filter's margin over persistence holds in both weightings. The
comparison with GRACE-FCast is not symmetric. Their training uses the gap
reconstruction of \citet{yin2023gtws}, whereas our models are fitted to
the observed series and this study's target definition. The 1-month
advantage also occurs for damped persistence. The external comparison
excludes fold 5 and basins without adequate forecast-grid coverage.

Finally, the evidence rests on two mascon products of one set of
observations, five test folds all in the post-2019 climate, and per-basin
% source: src/gracefc/evaluate.py DEFAULT_FOLDS (17 + 17 + 17 + 17 + 15 issue months at lead 1)
estimates based on 83 months at a 1-month lead time. The LSTM, MLP and
residual MLP were trained with the fixed architectures of
Sect.~\ref{sec:methods-corrections}, early stopping and no hyperparameter
search, with two seeds each for the first two and three for the third.
Table~\ref{tab:sequence} reports individual seeds, and the training-matched
comparison uses the LSTM seed ensemble. Under this budget, none has lower
CSR error than KF-R12E; whether further tuning changes this ordering
remains untested. The short record also limits inference about small
differences. Our uncertainty estimates account for overlapping forecasts,
but sensitivity to longer HAC bandwidths and bootstrap blocks has not been
evaluated.

\conclusions
\label{sec:conclusions}

For deseasonalized basin-average GRACE storage, the per-basin Kalman
forecast improves on the stronger damped-persistence variant at all six
tested leads on CSR and at 2 to 6 months on JPL. Refitting without an
observation-noise term removes the CSR 1-month advantage, supporting the
use of temporal filtering within this model family. We recommend reporting
skill against this benchmark alongside persistence and physical-unit errors.

A linear correction using twelve months of filtered storage and
ERA5-Land history has the lowest standardized CSR error at short leads
among the correction models tested. Its improvement is concentrated in
low-variance basins and does not extend to pooled error in centimeters.
GRACE-FCast has lower error at longer leads, whereas both KF and damped
persistence have lower error at 1 month. Any evaluation of storage
forecasts, including any future combination of storage-based and
forcing-based predictions, has to account for this dependence on lead
time, error scaling and input availability.
